title: The New Coke Fiasco
text:
In the early 1980s Coca-Cola was losing market share to Pepsi, whose advertising campaign, the Pepsi Challenge, showed ordinary people preferring Pepsi in blind sips. Coca-Cola's own research found the same thing: in sip tests, the sweeter Pepsi often won.

The company spent years developing a new, sweeter formula. In blind taste tests with roughly two hundred thousand people, the new recipe beat both old Coke and Pepsi. On 23 April 1985, chairman Roberto Goizueta announced that Coca-Cola was changing its formula, and the old one was taken off the market.

The reaction astonished the company. Tens of thousands of angry calls and letters poured in. People hoarded old Coke, a Seattle man organized a group called Old Cola Drinkers of America, and protesters poured the new drink into the streets. Many complainants said less about taste than about losing something that was part of their lives and of American identity. The taste tests had measured which drink people liked in one sip, not what they felt about the brand.

On 11 July 1985, less than three months after the launch, Coca-Cola announced that the original formula would return as Coca-Cola Classic. Sales of the old drink rose above their previous level, and the new formula slowly faded away.
lesson: Measuring the wrong thing can lead a careful process to a bad decision. Before changing something people love, ask what it means to them, not only how they rate it.
people: Roberto Goizueta, Donald Keough, Coca-Cola Company
source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993); Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986)
